summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, standing under the national framework of its Basic Law while administering its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity, and statutory non-discrimination protection extends only to employment, under Article 6(2) of Law 7/2008.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and a 2015 study of gender-marker change never produced legislation. On 7 April 2026 the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family law, and that there are no plans to revise the framework — an answer issued after four trans residents filed an appeal on 31 March 2026. Macau is the only area in China without provisions for identity-card gender-marker change or sex reassignment; both are available in mainland China and in Hong Kong.

The first organised push came in February 2015, when Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on identity documents. The individual making the request, identified as Avery, spoke from behind a screen. The practical consequence persists at the border: a trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered as female in Macau, producing confusion when crossing.

Protection from violence is excluded along the same line. A 2012 draft of domestic-violence legislation dropped same-sex cohabitants for "lack of social consensus", and the law enacted in 2016 left out same-sex partners because they were not treated as "family members". Rainbow of Macau criticised the exclusion in May 2016. A statement issued by Jason Chao for the association recorded that the government enacted the law with knowledge of the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination, and warned that the enactment signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

For a visitor: no exposure to prosecution, no recognition of gender or partnership, and no statutory recourse outside the employment sphere.
tangentialFactors:
Macau's position diverges sharply from both jurisdictions it is most often compared with. Gender-marker change and sex reassignment are legally possible in mainland China and in Hong Kong, leaving Macau as the sole area under the national framework where neither exists — a gap activists have pressed for years without a legislative result.

International scrutiny has produced commitments without effect. The UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations directed that protection from domestic violence be non-discriminatory; the 2016 law was enacted anyway, and the Justice Services Direction's April 2026 refusal to commit to reform shows the same pattern of review without revision.

Protection is narrow rather than absent: Law 7/2008 covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination in employment only, leaving housing, services, education and violence outside the statute, while the Basic Law's own discrimination list does not reach these grounds at all.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot alter the sex marker on their Macau identity cards, and no administrative route exists for doing so; the 2015 study of the question produced no law, and the Justice Services Direction said on 7 April 2026 that there are no plans to revise the framework. Four trans residents appealed on 31 March 2026, and local associations continue to press the promised legislative reform.

Same-sex couples are not recognised in marriage or partnership, and the 2016 domestic-violence law does not treat them as family, so a resident in a same-sex relationship has no claim under that statute. The 2012 draft's removal of same-sex cohabitants was justified publicly by a stated lack of social consensus.

Employment is the one field where residents hold a statutory non-discrimination claim, under Article 6(2) of Law 7/2008. Rainbow of Macau has acted as the principal body engaging government on identification documents and on the domestic-violence legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Macau has any hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provision covering anti-trans or homophobic violence, and no sourced statement covers facilities, bathroom access, or rules on gendered spaces.

No source addresses entry or visa screening of trans visitors, including whether immigration officers can question or refuse a traveller whose presentation differs from the sex marker on the document — the cross-border mismatch described here concerns a resident's identity cards, not border policy.

The content and recommendations of the 2015 gender-marker study are not sourced beyond the fact that it produced no law, and no timeline, legislative proposal or court ruling on gender recognition appears in the inventory. Enforcement of the employment protection in Law 7/2008 is likewise unverified here, as is any requirement, medical or otherwise, for persons seeking future recognition.
